level1.text: A disposable syringe contains $30.0\,\text{ml}$ of air at a pressure of $101\,\text{kPa}$. The tip of the syringe is closed with a finger, and the plunger is pulled out slowly until the volume of the air is $45.0\,\text{ml}$. The temperature of the air stays the same, and no air enters or leaves the syringe. What is the air pressure in the syringe now?

The pressure tank of a summer cottage's water system has a sealed air space at the top. When the tank has little water, the volume of the air is $24.0\,\textsf{l}$ and the total pressure is $160.0\,\text{kPa}$. The pump pumps more water into the tank, so the air is compressed and its total pressure rises to $280.0\,\text{kPa}$. The temperature of the air stays the same. What is the volume of the air now?

The graph shows example data: the pressure $p$ of the air in a disposable syringe as a function of the volume $V$, when the tip of the syringe is closed and the plunger is moved slowly, so the temperature of the air stays the same. What is the air pressure when its volume is $25\,\text{ml}$? Read the values you need from the graph.

A balloon at a birthday party contains $3.0\,\textsf{l}$ of air in a living room at $22\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The balloon is taken to the balcony in a frost of $-18\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, where its air cools to the temperature of the outside air. The air pressure in the balloon stays the same. What is the volume of the air in the balloon on the balcony?

The lid of a chest freezer is opened, and the air space of the freezer fills with room air at $22\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The lid is closed tight, so the air pressure in the freezer is $101\,\text{kPa}$. The air cools to $-18\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, and its volume stays the same. What is the air pressure in the freezer now? (This is why the lid is hard to open again right after closing it.)

A sealed amount of air is in a disposable syringe, and the plunger is moved slowly so that the temperature of the air stays the same. What does the graph look like in which the air pressure $p$ is plotted as a function of the volume $V$?
level1.answer: A falling curve, because the product $pV$ is constant and the pressure decreases as the volume increases.

choices.text: A falling straight line, because the pressure $p$ decreases by the same amount for every added millilitre.
choices.feedback: When the volume doubles, the pressure halves. If the graph were a straight line, the pressure would decrease by the same amount for every added millilitre, and it would drop to zero. In Boyle's law the pressure approaches zero but never reaches it.

choices.text: A rising straight line, because when the volume $V$ increases there are more particles in the air and the pressure increases.
choices.feedback: The amount of air sealed in stays the same all the time, so the number of particles does not increase. When the volume increases, the particles hit the walls less often and the pressure decreases.

choices.text: A falling curve, because the product $pV$ is constant and the pressure decreases as the volume increases.
choices.feedback: Correct: in an isothermal change $pV$ is constant, so $p = \text{constant} \cdot \dfrac{1}{V}$. The graph is a falling curve that approaches the axes but never meets them.

choices.text: A horizontal line, because the temperature $T$ is constant and therefore the pressure is constant too.
choices.feedback: A constant temperature does not mean a constant pressure. When the volume is changed, the rate at which particles hit the walls changes, so the pressure changes even though the temperature stays the same.

level1.text: The cylinder of an air compressor contains $1.50\,\textsf{l}$ of air at a pressure of $101\,\text{kPa}$. The plunger slowly compresses the air into a smaller space until the pressure is $240\,\text{kPa}$. The temperature of the air stays the same, and no air escapes from the cylinder. What is the volume of the air now?

A student measures the pressure $p$ of a sealed amount of air at different volumes $V$ at a constant temperature and plots the points in a $(1/V,\,p)$ graph. Within the measurement uncertainty, the points lie on a straight line through the origin. What does this show?
level1.answer: The pressure is inversely proportional to the volume, so the product $pV$ is constant.

choices.text: The pressure is directly proportional to the volume, because $1/V$ increases with the volume.
choices.feedback: When the volume increases, its reciprocal $1/V$ decreases. So a straight line in a $(1/V,\,p)$ graph means that the pressure is directly proportional to the reciprocal $1/V$, that is, inversely proportional to the volume.

choices.text: The temperature rose during the measurements, because the points $(V,\,p)$ are not on a curve.
choices.feedback: In the measurement the points $(1/V,\,p)$ were plotted, not the points $(V,\,p)$. If the temperature had risen, the points would not lie on a straight line through the origin but would deviate from it.

choices.text: The pressure is inversely proportional to the square of the volume, so the product $pV^2$ is constant.
choices.feedback: Then the points $(1/V,\,p)$ would lie on a curve, because $p$ would be directly proportional to the quantity $1/V^2$. A straight graph tells us that $p$ is directly proportional to the quantity $1/V$.

choices.text: The pressure is inversely proportional to the volume, so the product $pV$ is constant.
choices.feedback: Correct: a straight line through the origin means $p = k \cdot \dfrac{1}{V}$, and the slope is $k = pV$. Boyle's law holds within the measurement uncertainty.

level2.text: The cylinder of a firefighter's breathing apparatus has a volume of $6.8\,\textsf{l}$, and in a fully filled cylinder the air pressure is $300.0\,\text{bar}$ ($1\,\text{bar}$ = $100\,\text{kPa}$). How many cubic metres would this air take up if it were released to an atmospheric pressure of $101\,\text{kPa}$? The temperature stays the same. Assume that Boyle's law holds even at such a high pressure.

An empty glass bottle is closed with a cork at $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, so the air pressure in the bottle is $101\,\text{kPa}$. The bottle is forgotten on the sauna bench. The cork pops out when the air pressure in the bottle is $125\,\text{kPa}$. The volume of the bottle stays the same. At what temperature does the cork pop out? Give the answer in degrees Celsius.

In a physics lesson the tip of a disposable syringe was connected to a pressure gauge, and the plunger of the syringe was moved slowly so that the temperature of the air stayed the same. The measured volumes $V$ (ml) were 10.0; 12.5; 15.0; 20.0; 25.0 and 30.0, and the corresponding pressures $p$ (kPa) were 203; 159; 134; 99; 81 and 66. Calculate a column $1/V$ in the table, plot $p$ as a function of $1/V$ and fit a straight line through the origin to the points. The slope of the line is $pV$. Give it in joules.

The envelope of a hot-air balloon has a volume of $2800\,\text{m}^3$, and there is an opening at the bottom of the envelope. The envelope is full of air at $10\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, which is heated with a burner to $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The pressure inside the envelope stays equal to the outside air pressure. All the air that was originally in the envelope warms to $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. How many cubic metres of this $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ air do not fit in the envelope but have been pushed out through the opening?

Two sealed amounts of air are heated in a water bath. In vessel A the pressure $p$ of the air is measured and in vessel B the volume $V$ of the air. The air in both is at the temperature $\theta$ of the water bath (table, example data).

a) For every row of vessel A calculate the ratios $p/\theta$ and $p/T$, and for every row of vessel B the ratio $V/T$, where $T$ is the temperature in kelvins. Using your calculations, deduce which vessel shows an isochoric and which an isobaric change of state, and justify why the temperature must be in kelvins.

b) Predict the pressure of vessel A when the water bath boils and its temperature is $100\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

Write the result of part b) in the answer box.

data.caption: Air pressure in vessel A and volume in vessel B (example data)

level2.text:
A student verifies Boyle's law. She connects a disposable syringe to a pressure gauge with a thin hose and moves the plunger slowly so that the temperature stays the same. She reads the volume $V$ of the air from the scale of the syringe and the pressure $p$ from the gauge (table, example data). The student calculates the product $pV$ for every row and notices that it is not constant, although the temperature stayed the same. However, the hose and the gauge also contain air, whose volume $V_\text{h}$ is the same in all the measurements and which the student did not take into account.

a) Calculate the product $pV$ for every row and explain why it increases with the volume. Is the error random or systematic? Justify your answer.

b) The total volume of the sealed air is $V + V_\text{h}$, and Boyle's law holds for it. Determine the volume $V_\text{h}$ of the air in the hose and the gauge using the first and the last row of the table.

Write the result of part b) in the answer box.

data.caption: Air pressure as a function of the volume of the syringe (example data)

level2.text:
To determine absolute zero, a tight rigid bottle containing air is heated in a water bath, and the air pressure $p$ is measured as a function of the temperature $\theta$ (table, example data). The volume of the bottle and the amount of air stay the same.

a) Plot the points in a $(\theta,\,p)$ graph, fit a straight line to them and extend the line (extrapolate) to the pressure $p = 0$. What temperature in degrees Celsius do you get for absolute zero?

b) Compare the result with the known value $-273.15\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and explain why a real gas still does not reach this point, although the extension of the line passes through it.

Write the result of part a) in the answer box.

data.caption: Air pressure in a rigid bottle (example data)

level3.text: A diver is in a lake at a depth of $20.0\,\text{m}$ and blows an air bubble whose volume is $2.0\,\text{cm}^3$. The bubble rises to the surface. The atmospheric pressure is $101\,\text{kPa}$ and the density of water is $1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$. Assume that the temperature of the water is the same all the way and that the air of the bubble does not dissolve in water. What is the volume of the bubble at the surface? Using the result, justify why a person diving with compressed air must not hold their breath when rising to the surface.

The tyres of a car are filled in a garage at $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$, and the tyre pressure gauge shows $250.0\,\text{kPa}$. The gauge shows gauge pressure, that is, how much greater the air pressure in the tyre is than the atmospheric pressure. The atmospheric pressure is $101\,\text{kPa}$. At night the car stands in the yard, and the air in the tyre cools to $-20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The volume of the tyre stays practically the same, and no air escapes. What does the gauge show on a frosty morning? Justify why the reading of the gauge cannot be substituted directly into the formula $p_1/T_1 = p_2/T_2$.

The cylinder of a bicycle pump is $40.0\,\text{cm}$ long and equally wide along its whole length. When the plunger is pulled up, the cylinder is full of outside air at a pressure of $101\,\text{kPa}$. The gauge pressure of the tyre is $300.0\,\text{kPa}$. The valve of the pump lets air into the tyre only when the air pressure in the cylinder is equal to the air pressure in the tyre. How far must the plunger be pressed before air starts to flow into the tyre? Assume that the temperature stays the same and the volume of the hose is negligible. Justify why pumping a hard tyre feels inefficient.

A student studies air sealed in a disposable syringe. At first there is $40.0\,\text{ml}$ of air at a pressure of $101\,\text{kPa}$ and a temperature of $20.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. She compresses the air in two ways. In slow compression the temperature stays the same. In fast compression the plunger is pushed down in a fraction of a second and the pressure is read as soon as the plunger has stopped: the air has had time to give only part of the energy to the surroundings (table, example data).

a) Calculate the product $pV$ for every row in both series. Deduce in which compression Boyle's law holds.

b) Explain why the pressure in fast compression is greater than Boyle's law predicts. What happens to the pressure when the plunger is held still and the air cools back to the temperature $20.0\,{}^\circ\text{C}$?

c) Think of the fast compression as two steps: first an isothermal compression to the volume $10.0\,\text{ml}$ and then the warming of the air at constant volume to the pressure in the table. Use this to calculate the temperature of the air in degrees Celsius right after the fast compression, when the volume is $10.0\,\text{ml}$.

Write the result of part c) in the answer box.

data.caption: Air pressure in slow and fast compression (example data)

level3.text:
A freediver fills her lungs at the surface and dives into a lake holding her breath. The volume $V$ of the air in the lungs was measured at different depths $h$ (table, example data). The atmospheric pressure is $101\,\text{kPa}$, the density of water is $1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$ and $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$. Assume that the temperature and the amount of the air stay the same and that the pressure of the air in the lungs is all the time the same as the pressure of the surrounding water.

a) Calculate the total pressure $p$ of the surroundings at each depth and the product $pV$. Using your calculations, deduce whether the air in the lungs obeys Boyle's law.

b) Assume as a model that the lungs cannot be compressed to less than $1.5\,\textsf{l}$. At what depth would the volume of the air in the lungs reach this limit?

c) What is the ratio of the pressure at the depth of part b) to the pressure at the surface, and what is the ratio of the volumes of the lungs at the surface and at this depth? Compare the ratios.

Write the result of part b) in the answer box.

data.caption: Volume of air in a freediver's lungs (example data)
